---
title: "Red Dwarf Worlds"
---


Where most of humanity actually lives, and why almost none of its history was
written there.

`C-04` of the stars within reach of the Exodus are red dwarfs, and the fleet
aimed `C-07` hulls at the best of them (see [cosmography](/encyclopedia/cosmography.html)). The colonies that
survived became `C-15` of the founding settlements — the demographic bulk of the
species, on worlds that the Confederacy would later describe, without noticing
what it was saying, as the edge of things.

## The terminator

A red dwarf is dim, so its habitable zone lies close in. Close enough that tidal
forces win.

A world in that zone is locked: the same hemisphere faces the star forever. One
side is in permanent day, standing under a sun that never moves. The other is in
permanent night, and cold enough on the worst of these worlds that the
atmosphere itself weathers out onto the rock. Between them runs the terminator —
a ring of perpetual dusk, a few hundred kilometres wide, where the temperature
gradient is survivable and the light comes in sideways forever.

Everything lives in the ring.

This is the first fact of a red dwarf world and it shapes every other. A locked
world has no temperate band and no polar waste; it has an inside and an outside
and a habitable circle drawn between them. Cities are strung along the ring like
beads. Agriculture runs in the band where the light is strongest without being
lethal, which is the same band everyone wants to live in. Territory on such a
world is not an area. It is an arc, and an arc has exactly two directions to
expand in, and someone is already there.

The characteristic political geography of the diaspora's poorer half is a chain
of settlements that cannot grow sideways.

## A sky with no year in it

There are no seasons. A locked world has no axial tilt worth the name and no
meaningful orbital variation, so the light does not change. The sun does not
rise, does not set, and does not move. It hangs at a fixed angle that depends
only on where you stand, and you can navigate by it the way a sailor navigates
by a lighthouse.

Which means there is no year visible in the sky at all.

This is stranger than it sounds and its consequences run deep. A calendar has to
be *invented* rather than observed. On Earth and on the free-rotating worlds, the
year is a thing you notice; a child learns it before anyone teaches it. On a
locked world the orbital period is an astronomical abstraction that a
pre-industrial population has no way to perceive and no reason to care about.

So locked colonies keep time by whatever else recurs. Tidal cycles where there
is an ocean and a moon. Crop maturation, which fixes the calendar to the
agriculture rather than the other way round. Physiological rhythm, in
populations that kept a sleep cycle they no longer had a sun to hang it on.
Several kept the ship's clock — the arbitrary twenty-four-hour period their
Guide ran the first settlement on, preserved for millennia as a religious
inheritance nobody could account for.

The result is that the diaspora's poorer half does not share a unit of time with
its richer half, and did not until the Expansion Era imposed one. See
[stellar-calendar](/encyclopedia/stellar-calendar.html) for what that imposition cost.

## Flares

Red dwarfs are unstable in a way the Sun is not. They flare — irregularly,
violently, and across a spectrum that strips atmosphere and sterilises surfaces.
A world close enough to be warm is close enough to be scoured.

Nothing about this is survivable by prediction. Flare intervals are not periodic
and the warning is minutes at best. What is survivable is *architecture*: you
live under rock, or under water, or under enough engineered mass that the event
is a noise overhead rather than a death.

Every long-lived culture on a locked world is a culture that goes underground on
short notice and has organised itself around being able to. The shelter is the
civic building. The drill is the civic ritual. Populations that took millennia to
develop writing had flare protocol before they had law, because a settlement that
did not have it did not become a settlement.

And it is not superstition dressed as caution. A society whose central shared
experience is *the sky occasionally tries to kill everyone, without warning, and
the only response is to be already inside* produces a theology, and the theology
is remarkably consistent across worlds that never met. The star is not benevolent
and not malicious. It is awake, and it is indifferent, and you do not stand
under it longer than you need to.

Confederacy observers in the Expansion Era recorded these as sun-fearing
religions and filed them as primitive. They were engineering documents with
liturgy attached.

## Energy poverty, which decides everything

The rest of this entry describes texture. This part decides history.

**Red dwarfs are dim.** A world in the habitable zone of one receives enough
energy to be warm and nothing like enough to be rich. Every energy budget on
such a world is tighter than its equivalent on a free-rotating world around a
G-type sun: less incident light for agriculture, less for any solar
infrastructure, a thinner margin for everything built on top.

Less available energy means less foundry capacity. Less foundry capacity means a
lower industrial ceiling. And the Guide vaults release against *measured
industrial thresholds* — population, energy production, institutional stability
(see [guide-vaults](/encyclopedia/guide-vaults.html)).

So a locked colony does not merely develop more slowly. **It develops toward a
ceiling it may never reach, gated by a mechanism that cannot see why it is
failing.** The vault is not cruel and not broken. It is counting, and the numbers
do not arrive.

This is the mechanism behind the single most consequential asymmetry in galactic
history. The mobile colonies unlocked their corpus together, found each other,
and built the Confederacy. The locked colonies mostly did not, and were still
pre-industrial when the Confederacy arrived — which is why first contact between
branches of the diaspora was not a reunion but a **discovery**, asymmetric from
the first day, conducted by people who had a word for what they were doing and
had used it before.

See [galactic-timeline](/encyclopedia/galactic-timeline.html) for what the Expansion Era did with that advantage.

## Adaptation

A marginal-flight colony began with a narrower founder population than a primary
one — the manifest traded embryo mass for the adaptation corpus and the hardened
descent vehicles that would let anyone survive at all (see [cosmography](/encyclopedia/cosmography.html)).

Narrow founder populations, higher selective pressure, and a world demanding
irreversible modification: the outcome is divergence, fast and far. Adapted
populations change in stature, in colouring, in build, in the tolerances of the
skin and the eye — and because the direction of the change follows the world, no
two of them drift the same way. A population shaped by a dim sun and a permanent
sideways light does not resemble one shaped by a thin atmosphere and a
high-radiation ring, and neither resembles baseline human stock.

Under [sagan-kim-scale](/encyclopedia/sagan-kim-scale.html) this is what `I-14`'s second axis measures. A Tier 5
free world and a Tier 5 locked world are the same tier and not the same place,
and they do not produce the same people.

The social consequence is [sagan-kim-scale](/encyclopedia/sagan-kim-scale.html)'s to state. The historical one
belongs here: these populations cannot leave. Not by policy — biologically.
Adapted past compatibility with the worlds their cousins live on, they are bound
to the planet that made them, permanently, in a galaxy whose wealth is measured
in mobility.

## The long inheritance

One thing belongs to these worlds and to nothing else in the diaspora.

A G-type star has a working life of ten billion years. A red dwarf burns for a
trillion, and burns steadily for almost all of it. Every mobile colony in the
Confederacy is living on borrowed cosmic time by comparison; the locked worlds
are not.

The Exodus planners knew this, and it is why `C-07` hulls went to targets nobody
expected to work. A programme optimising for the next ten thousand years would
have sent everything to the good stars. This one did not.


::: {.callout-important collapse="true" title="Spoiler — click to open"}
Worth holding while reading the later eras: after the Great Scattering, when the
Nexus is gone and the mobile worlds are stranded in fragments, the locked
populations are exactly where they always were — on worlds no empire can reach,
around stars that will still be burning when every G-type sun in the former
Confederacy has gone out.

The Scattering did not scatter them. It left them alone, which is a different
thing, and in the very long run it may not be the worse one.
:::
